title: Scopes as types
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA)
solution: Treats scopes as types so scope graphs can model the internal structure of non-simple types (structural records, generic classes). Extends scope graphs with scoped relations and queries, and introduces Statix, a meta-language for static semantics based on scope graphs plus constraints.
methodology:
Abstract only (full text not read). The approach extends scope graphs with scoped relations and generalized queries and is realised in the Statix DSL, which specifies static semantics via scope graphs and constraints.
Evaluation, per the abstract, is by case studies: simply-typed lambda calculus with records, System F, and Featherweight Generic Java.
results: Abstract reports only that the approach and Statix design were evaluated in the three case studies; no quantitative figures are stated in the abstract.
gap: Our assessment: Scope graphs are a declarative, unbounded-memory model of name binding and resolution; it does not address a fixed byte buffer, LIFO push/pop of a hash table, probe limits, or the probability that an insertion is refused.

title: Knowing when to ask: sound scheduling of name resolution in type checkers derived from declarative specifications
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA)
solution: Gives a language-independent characterization (critical edges in an incomplete scope graph) of when name and type queries are stable, and uses it to define a small-step semantics for a declarative type-system specification language that delays unstable queries, yielding type checkers that are sound by construction.
methodology:
Abstract only. Formal characterization via critical edges; operational semantics of the specification language that delays queries which might depend on missing binding information.
Implemented and evaluated on specifications of a small module-and-record language and subsets of Java and Scala (as stated in the abstract).
results: Abstract claims necessary and sufficient conditions for query stability and soundness by construction; the abstract gives no performance numbers.
gap: Our assessment: Concerns when a lookup may be answered during checking (scheduling/ordering), not how declarations are stored; no bounded memory, no undo of scopes, no refusal probabilities.

title: Scope States: Guarding Safety of Name Resolution in Parallel Type Checkers
venue: 35th European Conference on Object-Oriented Programming (ECOOP 2021), LIPIcs vol. 194
verified_against: DataCite API (record + abstract; Crossref does not hold this DOI) and Schloss Dagstuhl page via WebFetch
solution: A framework for parallel hierarchical type checkers with dynamic, mutual dependencies between compilation units. A scope-graph name-resolution API plus a per-scope 'scope state' (completeness) lets cross-unit queries be delayed until safe, with no explicit synchronization code written by checker authors.
methodology:
Abstract only. Implemented in Java with the actor paradigm; used to parallelize the solver of Statix, so any Statix type checker with a split declaration/type specification style becomes parallel.
Evaluation by benchmarks on real-world code bases (details of the code bases not read).
results: Abstract reports speedups of up to 5.0x on 8 cores for the parallel Statix solver on real-world code bases.
gap: Our assessment: Targets multi-core speed of compile-time name resolution on desktop-class machines; says nothing about a single fixed buffer, LIFO scope discipline, or exact probabilities of a table refusing an insertion.

title: Incremental type-checking for free: using scope graphs to derive incremental type-checkers
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (OOPSLA2)
solution: Derives incremental type checkers automatically from Statix specifications: name-resolution queries in scope graphs define dependencies between compilation units, and a query-confirmation algorithm finds queries whose answers changed after an edit so only those units are re-analysed.
methodology:
Abstract only. Technique: dependency derivation from scope-graph queries, a query-confirmation algorithm, splitting checking into context-free and context-sensitive parts, and a generic mechanism for mutual dependencies.
Evaluation compares against non-incremental parallel execution on synthetic benchmarks and real-world projects.
results: Abstract reports speedups up to 147x on synthetic benchmarks and up to 21x on real-world projects over non-incremental parallel execution, with initial overhead below 10%.
gap: Our assessment: Incrementality is about re-checking after edits with unbounded memory; it does not cover bounded-memory tables, deterministic undo on scope exit, or refusal-probability guarantees.

notes: arXiv:2210.06121 is the extended edition; the Crossref record has no abstract.
title: Specializing Scope Graph Resolution Queries
venue: Proceedings of the 15th ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Software Language Engineering (SLE 2022)
verified_against: Crossref API (bibliographic record); abstract from arXiv:2210.06121 (extended edition, title 'Specializing Scope Graph Resolution Queries: Extended Edition')
solution: Removes a run-time bottleneck in Statix-derived type checkers (part of the name-resolution algorithm) by partial evaluation: a procedural intermediate query-resolution language and a specializer that translates declarative scope-graph queries into it.
methodology:
Abstract only (read via the arXiv extended edition; the ACM version's abstract was not directly accessible). Partial evaluation of declarative queries into a tailored intermediate language.
Evaluated by comparing type-checking run time on three benchmarks: Apache Commons CSV, IO and Lang3.
results: Abstract reports query resolution up to 7.7x faster and total type-checking run time reduced by 38-48%.
gap: Our assessment: Optimises the speed of scope-graph query resolution; does not consider memory-bounded storage of names, probe-limited hashing, or exact failure/refusal probabilities.

title: A Monadic Framework for Name Resolution in Multi-phased Type Checkers
venue: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Generative Programming: Concepts and Experiences (GPCE 2023)
verified_against: Crossref API (bibliographic record); abstract from Semantic Scholar Graph API
solution: A monadic interface for phased name resolution that detects and rejects checking runs where a name was resolved before its declaration was available, plus applicative functors that map syntax trees to phased monadic computations representing typing constraints.
methodology:
Abstract only. Techniques are a phase-aware monadic interface and applicative-functor-based compositional mapping over ASTs (building on Gibbons et al.).
Demonstrated by implementing type checkers for Mini-ML with Damas-Hindley-Milner inference and LM, a toy module language with a challenging import-resolution policy.
results: Abstract states the techniques narrow the gap between typing rules and multi-phased implementations and that phasing errors are detected; no quantitative evaluation is described in the abstract.
gap: Our assessment: Concerned with ordering/phases of name resolution in type checkers; no treatment of data-structure memory limits or table-level refusal behaviour.

title: Static TypeScript: an implementation of a static compiler for the TypeScript language
venue: Proceedings of the 16th ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Managed Programming Languages and Runtimes (MPLR 2019)
verified_against: Crossref API (bibliographic record, author order as in Crossref); abstract and parts of text from the Microsoft Research pre-publication draft PDF (marked 'MPLR 2019, Under submission')
read_level: abstract + parts of full text (pre-publication draft; final version may differ)
solution: Static TypeScript (STS), a TypeScript subset with a compiler/linker toolchain written in TypeScript running in the browser. Programs compile to ARM Thumb machine code linked against a precompiled C++ runtime, aimed at Cortex-M devices with 16-256 kB RAM (e.g. micro:bit, 16 kB).
methodology:
Read in the draft: description of the STS language subset (static layout of classes, nominal-style class compilation), the compilation scheme, and the MakeCode deployment context.
Evaluation compares STS (native Thumb and a VM) with C (gcc), Duktape, IoT.js, MicroPython, CPython and Node.js on STM32F401RE (96 kB RAM), ATSAMD51G19 (192 kB RAM) and a Raspberry Pi Zero (reference only), using small benchmarks including binary trees, richards, fann and nbody.
results: Draft states STS is over an order of magnitude faster than embedded interpreters on property-heavy benchmarks, less than 2x slower than Node.js there, interpreters run out of memory sooner, and STS runs on devices with as little as 16 kB RAM.
gap: Our assessment: Shows full compilation (including scoping and typing) targeting tiny devices but runs the compiler in a browser on the host; it does not give a fixed-buffer on-device symbol table or probabilistic analysis of its capacity limits.

title: WARDuino: a dynamic WebAssembly virtual machine for programming microcontrollers
venue: Proceedings of the 16th ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Managed Programming Languages and Runtimes (MPLR 2019)
verified_against: Crossref API (bibliographic record); abstract from Semantic Scholar Graph API
solution: Investigates WebAssembly for Arduino-compatible microcontrollers, extending a standard Wasm VM with safe live code updates, VM-level remote debugging, and configurable hardware modules to keep the VM footprint small.
methodology:
Abstract only. Design of the WARDuino VM extensions.
Evaluation, per the abstract, by a simple breakout game and micro-benchmarks compared with Espruino on ESP32.
results: Abstract states the VM runs approximately 5 times faster than Espruino, a JavaScript interpreter for the ESP32.
gap: Our assessment: A runtime for bounded-memory devices; compile-time scope handling and symbol-table capacity are outside its scope, and it offers no exact capacity/refusal analysis.

title: Interactive Programming for Microcontrollers by Offloading Dynamic Incremental Compilation
venue: Proceedings of the 21st ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Managed Programming Languages and Runtimes (MPLR 2024)
verified_against: Crossref API (bibliographic record); full-text PDF from the authors' lab site (static.csg.ci.i.u-tokyo.ac.jp)
solution: Offloads dynamic incremental compilation and linking to a host computer connected to the microcontroller, via BlueScript, a small language with an interactive (REPL-style) environment for ESP32, avoiding the memory footprint of on-device compilers.
methodology:
Compiler (TypeScript on Node.js, Babel parser) translates each submitted fragment to C, compiles with the ESP-IDF cross compiler, links, and sends the ELF to the device; the compiler keeps a global name table on the host so later fragments can reference earlier functions and globals.
Experiments on an M5Stack Fire (ESP32, 520 kB RAM) with a MacBook Pro host compare against MicroPython 1.19.1 and Espruino for execution speed and interactivity (benchmarks adapted from MakeCode tutorials).
results: Abstract reports BlueScript executes programs one to two orders of magnitude faster than MicroPython while interactivity is comparable to MicroPython.
gap: Our assessment: Avoids the on-device symbol-table problem by keeping the name table on the host; it therefore does not address compilers that must hold scoped names in a fixed on-device buffer with push/pop and refusal guarantees.

notes: arXiv id 2511.15821; Crossref issued date 2025-10-15, arXiv posted 2025-11-19.
title: BlueScript: A Disaggregated Virtual Machine for Microcontrollers
venue: The Art, Science, and Engineering of Programming
verified_against: Crossref API (bibliographic record) and arXiv API (id 2511.15821, abstract and journal_ref)
solution: Proposes a 'disaggregated' VM that offloads as many VM components as possible (incl. incremental and dynamic compilers) to a host, using a 'shadow machine' on the host that mirrors microcontroller execution state to cut communication overhead; instantiated as the BlueScript VM.
methodology:
Abstract only. Design and implementation of the BlueScript VM with host-side offloaded components and a shadow-machine data structure.
Experiments compare against MicroPython and Espruino (abstract level; setup details not read).
results: Abstract reports offloading does not seriously compromise expected benefits; the offloaded incremental compiler gives faster execution than MicroPython and Espruino with interactivity comparable to MicroPython, and the offloaded dynamic compiler improves VM performance.
gap: Our assessment: Argues for moving memory-hungry compiler state off the device; leaves open the case where scoped symbol tables must live on the device itself in one fixed buffer.

title: Femto-Containers: Lightweight Virtualization and Fault Isolation For Small Software Functions on Low-Power IoT Microcontrollers
venue: Proceedings of the 23rd ACM/IFIP International Middleware Conference (Middleware 2022)
verified_against: Crossref API (DOI record; Crossref title is the short 'Femto-containers') and arXiv API (id 2210.03432, full title, abstract, journal_ref)
solution: Femto-Containers: a middleware runtime (eBPF instruction set ported to microcontrollers, integrated in RIOT) for secure deployment, execution and isolation of small virtual software functions on low-power IoT devices over the network.
methodology:
Abstract only. Design and implementation in RIOT; the implementation is formally verified for fault isolation (RIOT shielded from code in a container).
Experiments on Arm Cortex-M, ESP32 and RISC-V microcontrollers measure memory footprint, energy and security trade-offs.
results: Abstract states the experiments show an attractive trade-off in memory-footprint overhead, energy consumption and security (no figures in the abstract text read).
gap: Our assessment: Representative of bounded-memory MCU runtimes with verified isolation; it is not about compilers or scoped symbol tables, so exact capacity/refusal behaviour of a fixed-buffer name table is untouched.
